title: My stock bot automatically adjusts its own trailing stops based on performance. Here’s how it works.
author: Cool_Big2955
selftext:
I’ve been building a hybrid trend-following/pullback bot for US stocks (Alpaca), and I recently added an adaptive learning layer that actually modifies its own parameters based on real trade outcomes. Instead of using static settings, the system analyzes closed trades with time-weighted scoring (newer trades count more) and automatically tunes itself.

The most impactful adjustment so far has been the self-adjusting trailing stop. Here is the logic:

If the time-weighted average gain from trailing-stop exits exceeds 5%, the bot increases the trailing stop percentage by 0.2% (up to a hard cap of 3.5%). This gives winning trends more room to breathe.

Conversely, if trailing stops are consistently resulting in losses, it tightens the trailing stop by 0.2% (down to a floor of 1.5%) to protect capital.

All adjustments are clamped within safe boundaries defined in the master config (.env). The adaptive layer can fine-tune, but never override or exceed the master safety limits.

It also learns which entry methods work best. If REVERSAL entries have a time-weighted win rate below 30% over at least 5 trades, it temporarily blocks that method entirely until it recovers. The same applies to PULLBACK entries. Validation prevents both methods from being blocked simultaneously.

This isn’t curve-fitting or overfitting to historical data — it’s real-time adaptation based on actual paper/live trade results. The system maintains a separate memory file for per-symbol statistics and applies symbol-specific overrides for RSI thresholds and ATR multipliers based on recent win rates and average PnL.

For example, after several weeks of paper trading, the bot autonomously increased its trailing stop from 2.0% to 2.2% because the time-weighted average gain from trailing exits was consistently above 5%. It didn’t need me to notice this pattern — it detected and acted on it itself.

I’m sharing this because I think most retail algo bots use completely static parameters, and I’d love to hear how others handle parameter adaptation. Are you using similar time-weighted learning? How do you prevent your adaptive systems from overfitting or drifting into unsafe territory?

Happy to share code snippets or discuss the validation logic in more detail.

\-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

check this out ;-)

Here is the core of the adaptive learning module. The bot analyzes its own closed trades using time-weighted scoring (recent trades carry more weight) and adjusts the trailing-stop parameters within strict limits:"



\# Time-weighted analysis - recent trades carry more weight than old ones

def \_calculate\_time\_weights(date\_series: pd.Series, half\_life\_days: int = 30) -> pd.Series:

now = datetime.now()

age\_days = (now - pd.to\_datetime(date\_series)).dt.total\_seconds() / 86400

weights = 0.5 \*\* (age\_days / half\_life\_days)

return weights.clip(lower=0.05)



\# Automatic adjustment of trailing stop based on actual results

trailing\_success = sales\[sales\["Action"\].str.contains("TRAILING", na=False)\]

if len(trailing\_success) >= 2:

weights = \_calculate\_time\_weights(trailing\_success\["Timestamp"\])

avg\_gain = \_weighted\_average(trailing\_success\["Return\_%"\], weights)



\# If trailing stops yield good returns, give the trend MORE room to breathe

if avg\_gain > 5 and params\["TRAILING\_STOP\_STOCK\_PCT"\] < 0.035:

new\_value = \_clamp(params\["TRAILING\_STOP\_STOCK\_PCT"\] + 0.002, "TRAILING\_STOP\_STOCK\_PCT")

params\["TRAILING\_STOP\_STOCK\_PCT"\] = new\_value

logger.info(f"Learned: Increasing trailing stop to {new\_value\*100:.1f}% (avg gain: {avg\_gain:.1f}%)")

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The line where you say this isn't overfitting because it's on real trades is the one I'd push on. Fitting to the last N closed trades is still fitting. You've swapped a large in sample for a tiny one, and a tiny one moves your stop on noise.

Five trades before blocking an entry method is the part that worries me most. A method that genuinely works will still hand you five bad ones in a row often enough that you end up switching it off right before it comes good.

The test that would convince me: freeze the adaptation, run the same period static, and compare on a stretch you never touched while building the adaptation rules. If the adaptive one doesn't win there, the layer is decoration.

replies.author: DesertClimber
replies.body:
That's basically what I do with my latest bots, all running in families with single-change variants tested against a control. Forward testing in a lab, with limited back tests.

I've been told it's still over fitting, however.

Maybe I don't understand their viewpoint- My current lab has logged over 64,000 trades across all variants- ALL forward testing, on daily, fresh OOS data (some on real money to determine fills, etc) ... and they still try to tell me it's all selection bias and overfitting, and that I don't understand variance, etc. LOL

I mean, of course it's a little bit of selection bias. I'm not going to pick the worst performer and throw it on real money. But I also don't pick the best performer if it seems over fit to the regime or data I can test it against.

Most of the hard-core naysayers probably analyze something to death, and never actually implement anything, is my guess.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: The overfit charge only really lands if you pick the best variant out of the family afterwards and then quote its numbers like you'd chosen it up front. Running the whole family forward against a control is the opposite of that. What does quietly overfit you is retiring the losers and not counting them.

replies.author: DesertClimber
replies.body:
Good point.  
  
The losers don't get retired, but rather I keep all variants continuously running & logging trades every day on fresh data- even though a winner was picked to run live on elevated risk %, the lab still runs and gets analyzed at least weekly.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: The trap in that is comparing them on money. The live one runs at elevated risk and the lab ones don't, so per trade R is the only comparison that survives the sizing difference. Keeping the losers running is the counterfactual most people throw away.

replies.author: DesertClimber
replies.body:
I don't think the money really makes much of a difference, personally. A 25% account gain... is still a 25% account gain, I personally feel. Whether trade sizes are $100 on paper or $1000 live money, I generally look at how much it was right vs wrong- not the $ amount. (accounting for fees/spread, etc)  
  
EXCEPT when a strategy in compounding on a bankroll % of the entire account balance. That's when I think the results skew. But the right call vs wrong call for the strategy's decisions are still the same numbers in my mind.

Unless you're really just pointing out people throw away the losers, and never have the true comparison? That's not something I do.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
The percentage is the same, the fills are not. At $100 you sit inside the top of book every time. At $1000 on a thin instrument you start eating levels, and that comes straight out of the same percentage you are measuring.

Size is a strategy parameter, not an accounting detail.

replies.author: DesertClimber
replies.body: Yes, that's definitely a consideration depending on the book. One of my strats locks at a certain level, regardless of the account size it's trading on for that very reason.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: laddered resting limits is a decent dodge, though it does change what you're measuring. you stop testing the signal on its own and start testing signal plus fill luck, which is fine as long as you know that's the number you're looking at.

replies.author: DesertClimber
replies.body:
The latest lab runs 18 families, with 104 total variants, all working on the same instrument concurrently, with 5 of those running live on real money getting analyzed.  
  
Lots of data to work with. More than most, I would say- and this was to create just the most recent strategy I run.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 104 variants on one instrument is not 104 experiments though. they all see the same price path, so picking the winner is picking whichever one fit that one path best. that is the overfitting people mean. the number of trades went up, the number of independent things you tested did not.

replies.author: DesertClimber
replies.body:
True, but all testing against a control(s) is the only way to determine what works for that instrument.

Every market & instrument behaves differently, so one strategy built for an active, 24/7 market like Bitcoin won't work the same as say, with an instrument like ES.

Each market has to be tested individually with their own family of strategies (or a family across instrument), and then be cross-validated.

Or at least, that's how I handle it.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Running a family per instrument is where the control needs the most care. Fit a family to ES, pick its winner, then do it again for BTC, and the number of variants you ran is part of the result. Almost nobody logs that count, and it's the thing that makes a control honest.

replies.author: DesertClimber
replies.body: Agreed, that's why all my lab sets just keep rolling, losers included. Once you've got the data coming in live for a few instruments/markets, it's just a log file that can be parsed against later. Plenty of drive space, so why not store everything.  :)

replies.author: Endscapes-01
replies.body: This is how I handle as well, even on SPX vs NDX, I found more opportunities to mean revert selling call credit spreads on NDX despite SPX having similar move patterns
